Motion capture games · 10 November 2026 · Operator controls

Choose the camera.
Keep capture explicit.

The tracking console, Mole Motion and Dodgeball now share a named camera selector and Refresh control. The connected EMEET USB camera was selected and opened successfully with RTMPose; no participant images were saved.

Issue #23 · Owning camera guide · Verification results

Problem and resulting behavior

Previously, browser camera discovery revealed names but native capture still required an unrelated numeric index. The new Choose camera field lists native device names directly. Refresh detects newly connected cameras without opening them. Choose a device, then Start camera. Stop unlocks selection for switching. The console keeps optional browser identification in a secondary section; the manual index is available only through an explicit advanced choice.

Identity, ownership and recovery

  • The local vision service owns enumeration and capture. The UI never guesses an OpenCV index from browser order and never opens a second gameplay camera.
  • Opaque device references are derived from OS identity and the capture backend. Start re-resolves the selected identity before replacing a source and again after model loading. Reordering therefore does not reuse an old index; a missing selection raises an error.
  • Refresh retains a still-connected choice, clears a removed choice and never chooses a replacement. Multiple initially available devices require a choice. A single initially available device is preselected; capture still needs an explicit Start. Duplicate names are numbered, and names are rendered as text.
  • Discovery is bounded to 32 devices in a fresh serialized subprocess with a ten-second deadline. Browser requests expire after twelve seconds. Metadata enumeration reads no images; loading, empty, disconnect and service-error states remain visible and recoverable.
  • Manual indices retain their existing 0–9 range and have no stable identity guarantee. RTMPose defaults, camera ownership, source epochs, session membership and scoring behavior remain intact.

macOS enumeration mirrors the pinned OpenCV 4.11 AVFoundation video/muxed list and unique-ID sort. Windows uses Media Foundation metadata from pinned cv2-enumerate-cameras 1.4.0. The package installs its AVFoundation bridge only on macOS. Raw OS device paths/serials are not sent to the browser or embedded here. Linux named discovery is outside this slice; manual selection remains available.

New synthetic cases cover duplicate names and private paths, identity reordering/removal, rejection before stopping an existing source, re-resolution after model load, malformed discovery output, driver failures/timeouts, read-only list/origin rules, selection locking, manual validation and late discovery results. Existing game lifecycle tests now use named camera choices and continue to verify admission/release safety.

USB hardware spot check

After the user reconnected the camera, macOS and the native endpoint listed EMEET SmartCam C960 4K and MacBook Air Camera. The real browser selector opened EMEET with RTMPose and delivered a 960 × 540 preview. One sample after five seconds showed 60.0 render FPS, 30.3 camera/source FPS and 30.3 observation updates/sec, with no people detected. This establishes enumeration and live capture for this connection only. It is not an accuracy, 4K/60 sensor-mode or sustained latency certification. No camera images were saved or embedded.

Before and after

The before images are the prior console's generated three-body performance screenshots. After images use synthetic camera names supplied to the real dev-server UI while capture is stopped. They demonstrate controls and recovery, not the number of physical devices attached. All media is embedded for offline viewing.

Reproduce and use

pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm check
pnpm build
pnpm dev

Open http://127.0.0.1:5173
Choose camera → select the device → Start camera
Stop → choose another camera → Start camera
Reconnect USB devices → Refresh

Remaining limitations

macOS camera/accessory permission and a working data/power connection are still required. Software cannot list USB devices the OS has not exposed. Only one camera is active at a time. Windows physical capture, simultaneous camera modes, calibrated fusion, real participant accuracy and external motion-to-display latency remain unverified. OpenCV opens a native index, so changing hardware between the final identity check and acquisition retains a small OS hot-plug race; stop/reconnect/Refresh after errors. No calibration or player identity is inferred from this selector.
